title: Funds want advice reform action soon
full_text:
Three of Australia's biggest superannuation funds are pushing the Albanese government to accelerate the implementation of long-dormant financial advice reforms, placing renewed pressure on Assistant Treasurer Daniel Mulino to address the limited ways they can guide ageing, uncertain members through retirement.
Aware Super chief executive Deanne Stewart, UniSuper chief advice officer Andrew Gregory and Rest Super executive Simone Van Veen - representing funds that collectively manage $500 billion of retirement assets - voiced their strong support for an overhaul of advice laws that have languished in draft form since March 2025.
The changes are part of the Delivering Better Financial Outcomes package, itself a response to a review from early 2023.
That review, chaired by Michelle Levy, recommended allowing super funds to charge members for a wider range of advice and introducing a new class of advisers who could give tailored guidance at a lower cost for members who could not afford or access planning services.
But, as it stands, funds are not allowed to proactively contact their members and inform them of more appropriate investment options or account types. They also cannot consider a person's broader circumstances outside their super account without charging thousands of dollars.
The issue has become a major focus for funds as they prepare for 2.5 million people to retire over the next decade, many with substantial super balances, and wealthier customers seek more bespoke advice or solutions outside the traditional system.
Aware Super's Stewart, whose fund is the third-largest in the country, said the second stage of the advice reforms that focused on what advice can be provided through super funds and banks should be implemented as soon as possible. Although Aware employed 100 advisers and had rolled out several digital advice tools, she said further, more useful developments were impaired without the long-mooted changes.
"The reforms will enable us to further expand the range of advice we can offer and will give us greater ability to proactively advise our members on what they can do to achieve their retirement goals."
The comments were echoed by UniSuper's Gregory, who said financial advice services and laws had not kept pace with the rapid growth of Australia's $4.5 trillion super system, and Rest chief member officer Van Veen.
"The advice reforms are a once-in-a-generation opportunity to improve access to financial guidance for millions of Australians by creating more pathways to advice," Gregory said.
"Across the industry we are talking about millions of Australians, so removing these hurdles must be a priority because we know that members who receive advice have better retirement outcomes."
Van Veen said his fund had "previously urged government to progress these important measures". In a pre-budget submission from January, Rest even pushed Mulino and the government to "urgently legislate" the measures.
"At a time when many Australians face increasingly complex retirement decisions, reforms that expand access to affordable, quality advice are an important step forward," he said.
The comments come after AustralianSuper became the latest major fund to secure a licence to provide financial advice this month and detailed to The Australian Financial Review its plans to spin up a new advice business with Levy as a director.
About 2.5 million Australians are projected to retire over the next decade, many with substantial superannuation balances that have accrued over 30 years, and who are seeking advice and guidance for retirement.
Industry funds are already seeing older, wealthier members withdraw their money with the help of a financial adviser, who are directing them to newer wealth platforms that offer much more bespoke retirement products.
Mulino declined to comment on Tuesday. He will address the National Press Club next week, where he will unveil the government's policy response to the $1 billion failure of the Shield and First Guardian Master Funds and is also expected to provide an update on the progress of the advice reforms.
David Bell, the managing director of the Conexus Institute retirement think tank, said that advice provided by the funds could be sceptically viewed as a member retention tool, but would lead to better outcomes for those members who"cannot or will not access more comprehensive advice".
The existing laws, however, were "grey at best and for many prohibitive to providing a collectively charged personal advice offering," he said. "
Funds have the opportunity to provide a scaled advice service which meets the broad needs of many at low cost, and potentially no explicit cost."
The chief executive of the Association of Super Funds of Australia, Mary Delahunty, said funds needed "clarity on the line between general and personal advice, on how they can use digital tools, and on how to discuss things like the age pension and transition to retirement strategies with their members".
Delahunty said the stalled tranche of reforms would clarify how funds could "nudge" or suggest to members that they take up more suitable products, expand what can be collectively charged and simplify the process for funds.
